clue.text: Kipling's drink for you, parson?

parts.note: Kipling's poem A Smuggler's Song promises a particular spirit for the parson and tobacco for the clerk

explanation.surface: A question offering a clergyman the drink a famous poet allotted him.
explanation.definitionFit: The smugglers in Kipling's poem leave this spirit for the parson, a cognac-style liquor distilled from wine.

clue.text: They're just right for boxing compasses

definitions.text: They're just right for boxing compasses

parts.words: They're just right for boxing compasses
parts.note: the reading is of cases built to house a ship's steering compass, not of a fight

explanation.surface: Something ideal for putting drawing instruments in a box.
explanation.definitionFit: On a ship, the compass sits in a housing stand near the helm, which encloses it like a box.

clue.text: Dancing girl can turn up for record in time

parts.note: an alma (almah) is an Egyptian dancing girl

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning something up reads its letters from the bottom, so backwards

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A dancer kicks a can in the air.
explanation.definitionFit: An annual publication records dates, tides and events through the year: a calendar-based record.

clue.text: "Go socialist" upset a Conservative — so disparaging!

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset means the quoted words are flipped over and read upwards

parts.note: taken as written
red is the colour of socialism, so a socialist is a red
a Tory is a member of Britain's Conservative Party

explanation.surface: A Tory is outraged at being told to turn left and finds the remark insulting.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe remarks that belittle or run down their target.

clue.text: Give Les a drop — suffering cats !

indicators.note: something suffering is in a bad way, so these letters are knocked out of their order

explanation.surface: Someone asks for a tot for poor Les, exclaiming at their luck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'suffering cats!' reads as an old exclamation, but 'cats' is the definition; the anagram of LES A DROP gives the spotted big cats.
explanation.definitionFit: Leopards are spotted big cats of Africa and Asia.

clue.text: In revised text pirate is the look-out man

indicators.note: one piece is placed inside the other, as the clue puts the pirate in the text
revised text has been reworked, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: a rover is an old word for a pirate or sea robber

explanation.surface: In an edited script, a pirate is cast as the ship's lookout.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revised' turns TEXT into EXT...T, and 'In' puts ROVER inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: An outgoing person directs attention outwards, so the setter calls such a person one who looks out.

clue.text: Agreement in the bag, say ?

indicators.note: say signals that the phrase is to be heard rather than spelt

parts.note: things in the bag have been packed

explanation.surface: A deal that is already settled, as good as in the bag.
explanation.definitionFit: A pact is a formal agreement or treaty between parties.

clue.text: Nesbit children brought up on these lines

definitions.text: Nesbit children brought up on these lines

parts.words: Nesbit children brought up on these lines
parts.note: E. Nesbit's novel names its child heroes after the tracks beside which they grew up

explanation.surface: Children in a Nesbit story raised according to certain principles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on these lines' sounds like 'in this way', but it means tracks: Nesbit's book is The Railway Children.
explanation.definitionFit: Nesbit's children live beside train tracks, and those tracks are the lines meant.

clue.text: As sweet as this to loaf in Rio?

definitions.text: As sweet as this to loaf in Rio?

parts.words: As sweet as this to loaf in Rio?
parts.note: the phrase sweet as ... is joined to Rio's famous mountain called a loaf

explanation.surface: Wondering how pleasant it would be to laze around in Rio.
explanation.walkthrough: 'loaf' looks like lazing about, but Rio de Janeiro has the Sugar Loaf mountain; and 'sweet as' completes the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: The sweetener names both the simile and the conical mountain overlooking Rio's harbour.

clue.text: Bird talk

definitions.meaning: a small songbird such as the stonechat

explanation.definitionFit: The name of a small songbird is also an informal word for conversation.

clue.text: No military music for the Greek governor

parts.note: a march is music for soldiers to walk in step to

explanation.surface: A Greek official bans the military band.
explanation.definitionFit: In modern Greece a provincial district was a nome, run by an appointed head.

clue.text: Union leader at the gathering

parts.note: the TUC is Britain's Trades Union Congress
a king leads his people

explanation.surface: A union boss addresses a meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gathering' looks like a meeting, but it is the dressmaker's sense of folding cloth into pleats.
explanation.definitionFit: In sewing, small folds stitched into fabric draw it in, a kind of gathering.

clue.text: A bad beating? No, a denial is issued

indicators.note: a bad version of these words is a corrupted one, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a beating was bad and an official denial follows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bad' rearranges BEATING and NO into BNEGATION, which follows the opening A.
explanation.definitionFit: Self-denial or renunciation; refusing oneself something.

clue.text: Jug the fair-minded Bill and Jan each held in his own name

definitions.text: Jug the fair-minded Bill and Jan each held in his own name

parts.words: Jug the fair-minded Bill and Jan each held in his own name
parts.note: Bill ... and Jan ... ride to Widecombe Fair in the folk song, and each surname ends in the same four-letter vessel

explanation.surface: Two honest men called Bill and Jan each owned a jug under their own name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fair-minded' looks like 'just', but it means bound for Widecombe Fair, an English folk song listing Bill Brewer and Jan Stewer.
explanation.definitionFit: A large pitcher with a wide spout, once used for washing water.

clue.text: Where one new caller gets fuddled?

definitions.text: Where one new caller gets fuddled?

indicators.note: fuddled means muddled with drink, so these letters are mixed up

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A visitor arrives and gets drunk somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition too: a newcomer to a cellar of bottles might well get fuddled.
explanation.definitionFit: A cellar stocked with bottles is just the place a visitor might get tipsy.

clue.text: Placed a pass back to Edward

indicators.note: back means the first two pieces are read in the opposite direction

parts.note: a col is a mountain pass
Ted is a short form of the name Edward

explanation.surface: A footballer knocks the ball back to a teammate called Edward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns A COL into LOCA, then TED follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Both mean situated or put in a particular position.

clue.text: Note the union found trifling

parts.note: D is a musical note
an alliance is a union of parties or states

explanation.surface: A memo says the union was judged unimportant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trifling' looks like an adjective but is a noun here, flirting or idle toying.
explanation.definitionFit: Idle flirtation or toying with something rather than taking it seriously.

clue.text: The Avengers featured her in yesterday's showing

indicators.note: something featured in the words appears inside them, read straight through

explanation.surface: A TV review of The Avengers says a certain actress appeared in yesterday's episode.
explanation.walkthrough: The Avengers suggests the TV series; it means the Furies of Greek myth.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the Furies were goddesses who avenged crimes, especially murder within families.

clue.text: Birds of the air ?

parts.note: an air is also a tune, so these birds are the ones who sing

explanation.surface: Birds that fly in the sky.
explanation.definitionFit: Songbirds, and people who sing, both produce airs or tunes.

clue.text: Separate a number — not many

definitions.meaning: distinct or individual, as in the legal phrase joint and individual liability
more than two but not a lot

explanation.definitionFit: The word means individual or distinct, and also a small handful, more than two but not many.

clue.text: Baddy is bad without effect

annotationWithheld.why: 'Baddy is bad without effect' (7): VILLAIN is ILL inside VAIN, but 'without' must be both the container indicator and part of 'without effect' for VAIN, one word doing two jobs

clue.text: Change her note on that

indicators.note: change tells us to alter the order of these letters

explanation.surface: A musician is told to alter the note she sings.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal word meaning upon that thing or immediately after it.

clue.text: Rival gets bird-strange tale

parts.note: the emu is a large flightless Australian bird

indicators.note: strange signals the letters are put into an odd new order

explanation.surface: A competitor hears an odd story about a bird.
explanation.definitionFit: To rival someone is to try to equal or outdo them, as in imitating to match.

clue.text: Mark the fighter in the ring

annotationWithheld.why: 'Mark the fighter in the ring' (4) for BOLT: no parse found linking 'Mark' or 'the fighter in the ring' to the answer
annotationWithheld.clue: Mark the fighter in the ring

clue.text: Francis who turned up without a taxi

indicators.note: in a down clue, turned up means the letters are read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: without a taxi is no cab

explanation.surface: Someone named Francis arrived without having taken a cab.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned up' looks like 'arrived', but it reverses NO CAB.
explanation.definitionFit: Francis Bacon was the Elizabethan philosopher and statesman, also a twentieth-century painter.

clue.text: Small arms repeaters?

parts.note: small reads as tiny, and repeaters as guns fired at regular sixty-second intervals as a signal or salute

explanation.surface: A question about repeating rifles or pistols.
explanation.definitionFit: Signal guns fired once every sixty seconds, at funerals or by ships in distress; tiny is another sense of the first word.

clue.text: Sound unsatisfied with union leader's rate?

indicators.note: the leader of the word union is its first letter

parts.note: mph, miles per hour, is a rate of speed

explanation.surface: Someone grumbles about the speed the union boss is going at.
explanation.definitionFit: An interjection voicing dissatisfaction or doubt, like a grunt.

clue.text: Forget to order it .-

parts.note: the OM is the Order of Merit, a British honour

explanation.surface: Someone is told to forget about ordering it.
explanation.definitionFit: To leave something out or fail to do it, as through forgetting.

clue.text: Poet or commercial traveller?

definitions.meaning: George ... was an Elizabethan poet who translated Homer
an old word for a pedlar or itinerant dealer

explanation.definitionFit: George Chapman was the Elizabethan poet who translated Homer; the common noun is an old word for a pedlar.

clue.text: Plunder from the beach about one pound

indicators.note: about means the beach word goes round the next two pieces

parts.note: plage is a French word for a beach, also used in English
I is the Roman numeral one
L is the abbreviation for a pound, from Latin libra

explanation.surface: Loot is taken from the seashore worth around a pound.
explanation.definitionFit: Both mean looting or violently stealing goods, especially in war.

clue.text: Number of garrulous people

parts.note: chatterboxes are said to talk at this many to the dozen

explanation.surface: How many talkative people are present.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'talk this many to the dozen' describes someone who chatters non-stop.

clue.text: People to fear at the present time

definitions.text: People to fear at the present time

parts.words: People to fear at the present time
parts.note: Virgil's line warns to fear Danaans even when bearing gifts, so present means a gift

explanation.surface: Those who are dangerous nowadays.
explanation.walkthrough: 'present time' suggests now, but present means a gift: 'beware of Greeks bearing gifts' (Virgil, Aeneid).
explanation.definitionFit: The Trojan Horse was the Greeks' gift, hence the proverb to fear them bearing presents.
